title: Product photography for a florist
metaTitle: Photograph the flowers you can sell
excerpt: Photograph the flowers you can sell this week, in one crop and one background. Retire the file when the offer ends so the grid stays honest.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass, the weekly promise a florist's pictures have to keep.
caption: A shop window stating what is open, not what used to be. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a florist photograph an arrangement?
faqs.answer: Shoot it when the offer goes live, or the evening before, and only if the picture matches what you will deliver. A frame from an earlier week is a different product. If the market forces a substitution, change the picture or say exactly what may change.

faqs.question: How do you keep a florist's photo grid consistent?
faqs.answer: Use one crop, one background, and light from the same side, so sizes can be compared. The grid image should show the whole bunch or vase. Detail shots can live lower on the page, after the full offer is clear.

faqs.question: Should old flower photos stay on the product page?
faqs.answer: Remove them from the shop when the offer ends. You can keep the file in an archive and label the month if you show it later as past work. Do not put a new date on last season's photograph and call it this week.

markdown:
A florist product photography practice has to show what is available this week. A permanent catalog of every stem you have ever held will outlive the flowers and train customers to expect a picture you cannot repeat. Shoot the week's work, in one crop and one background, and retire the file when the offer ends.

The grid is a set. Mixed crops, mixed tables, and last month's wedding photo dropped into a row of wrapped bunches make the shop look unfinished. Consistency is the brand. Novelty is how the week stays true.

## Photograph the week you can sell

Before you shoot, write the list of live offers. Each offer gets pictures. Anything not on the list does not get a turn on the shop grid, however beautiful it was on Saturday.

Match the frame to the promise. A wrapped bunch is photographed as a wrapped bunch, at the size you will deliver. A vase arrangement is photographed in the vessel the customer will receive, or in one you have stated is a stand-in of the same scale. A single stem, sold as a single stem, should not be styled into a centerpiece and then priced as one stem.

Shoot on the day the offer goes live, or the evening before. Flowers move. A photograph from a softer morning, used three days later, is a different product. If you must shoot earlier, say so only if the picture still matches. When it does not, reshoot. The cost of a bad frame is an order you have to apologize for.

Weddings and events can live in a separate set, clearly labeled as work you have done, without a buy button. Those pictures are a portfolio. They are not this week's shop. Putting a bridal bouquet in the same grid as a twenty-dollar bunch confuses the price, the scale, and the lead time.

If the market forces a substitution, the picture has to change with it, or the page has to say the palette is the promise and the species may shift. Do not leave Friday's ranunculus up as the picture for Monday's tulips because the colors were "close."

## One crop so the row holds

Choose one crop for the shop grid and keep it. A square, or a consistent portrait, with the flowers occupying the same share of the frame. The eye should be able to compare size across the row. If one bunch is shot from the ceiling and the next is a tight crop of petals, the prices become impossible to judge.

The background stays put. A wall, a table, a paper. One of them. Flower color is already loud. A new backdrop every week makes the shop look like a different company, and it hides the only comparison that matters: the flowers themselves.

Light from the same side. Morning window light is enough if you can return to it. A ring light for one item and a window for the next will show up as a stripe of disagreement down the page. On dark days, have a backup you have already tested, or wait. Publishing a gray, muddy frame because the schedule said "post by nine" is how trust erodes in small steps.

Leave a margin so stems are not cut off at the top unless the crop is deliberately a detail. Detail frames are allowed. They are not the grid image. The grid image shows the whole offer, because the whole offer is what the person is buying.

Write the crop on a card: distance from the table, height of the camera, which wall. The person who photographs next Monday may not be the person who photographed this one. The card is the system. Taste still decides which bunch is worth a picture. The card decides whether that picture can sit beside the others.

## Scale, vessel, and the hand

People misread flower pictures. A tight crop makes a small bunch look like a monument. An overhead shot makes a tall vase look like a plate. Pick the angle that tells the truth about scale, and use it every week.

Put a vessel in the frame when the vessel is part of the sale. If the customer keeps only the flowers, photograph the bunch as it will be handed over, tied the way you tie it, paper you actually use. If you include a vase, the vase in the picture is the vase they get, or the page says otherwise in the first lines.

A hand can show scale when you do not want a ruler in the frame. The same person, or at least the same way of holding, so the hand does not become a new variable. A huge crop of a single bloom, with no hand and no bunch, is a poster. Use it as a detail, lower on the page, after the full offer is visible.

Color is a fact. White flowers go gray when the exposure is wrong, and red flowers clip into a flat shape. Expose for the petals, not for a moody shadow. You can still have a quiet picture. You cannot have a picture that invents a color the market did not sell you.

If you sell two sizes, photograph both, in the same setup, the same morning. Writing "larger option available" under one heroic frame pushes the decision into guesswork. Two frames, two prices.

## Retire the file with the flowers

A photograph of a perishable good has a shelf life. When the offer ends, take the picture off the shop. Keeping it because it performed well is how you sell a ghost.

Store the retired files in a folder that is not the live grid. You may use one of them later in a note about the season, labeled with the month. You may not quietly reuse it as "this week" the next time those stems appear, unless you have shot the new bunch and it truly matches. Even then, a new file is safer. Customers screenshot.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks you not to treat a page as fresh when the substance has not changed, and it asks whether the result is something you would still recommend. A product page with a new date and last spring's photograph fails that test in a way a buyer can see. Update the picture, or do not pretend the page is current.

Do not burn the week into the image. No date stamp, no "Mother's Day" script across the peonies, no price in the pixels. Those belong in the page, where you can change them without reshooting. A price baked into a photograph will be wrong the moment you edit the offer, and it will still be circulating in someone's camera roll.

Alt text should name the offer and the week in ordinary language: "Wrapped white and green bunch, kitchen-table size, this week's shop." When the offer retires, the alt retires with the page. A leftover description of peonies on a page about branches is the same lie as the leftover picture.

## A Monday shot list

Keep it short enough to finish before the shop opens to orders.

1. The full offer, shared crop, shared background, whole bunch or whole vase.
2. A second frame only if scale is hard to read, with the hand or the vessel you always use.
3. One detail of a bloom or a tie, if the page needs it, clearly not the grid image.
4. The card and the paper, only on the days they are new. Otherwise reuse the plain description in type.

Name files by the offer and the date. Delete the soft ones, the ones with a bucket in the background, and the ones that crop off the bow you consider part of the product. Export at the size the site will use so you are judging the real thumbnail, not the camera's flattery.

Check the row on a phone before you open checkout. If one tile is darker, tighter, or shot on a different table, fix it now. The person ordering from a doorway will not forgive a muddled row because the flowers themselves were good.

If a holiday week needs more offers, shoot them into the same system. More pictures, same crop. A holiday is not a reason to invent a second visual brand for seven days. You can change the paper and the palette. You should not change the frame, the type, and the background in the same morning.

## The unfinished grid

An unfinished florist grid has a familiar cause. Wedding work beside daily bunches. A portrait of the owner beside a top-down flat lay beside a window selfie. All of them can be good pictures. They cannot be one row.

Make two homes if you need both kinds of pictures. The shop row is this week, one crop. The story of the studio can be a single larger frame elsewhere on the site, or a short page about the shop, updated when you mean it. The buy buttons live only with the weekly row.

Look at the backgrounds as a strip. If you can name three surfaces, you have three brands. Pick the one that makes the flowers easiest to see, and reshoot the odd tiles, or remove them until you can.

This is the same restraint a jewelry studio needs, for a different reason. The object is small, the price is considered, and the picture has to carry detail and scale without a new backdrop for every piece.
